items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, they’ve all said there was nobody like Armstrong and they all copied and learned from him.

ctx.x: Yeah if you listen to “West End Blues” I think that’s all you need to hear to back up that statement.

Yup. And it’s interesting on “West End Blues” he uses that wordless vocal in the latter part of the recording, which is perfectly in keeping with what he has played. I love that record as an example of Armstrong as the complete lyric performer and the great technician as well. The fact that he sings a vocal that has no words is completely fitting to that aspect of his work, because the words don’t make any difference and he treats the words like that in many of his vocal performances. And yet when he wants to…
Do you suppose that performance, and especially that introduction was completely spontaneous?

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I knew that her aunt was – oh, who was that woman? Ella, a musical comedy star. Ella Logan.

ctx.x: Because I’ve talked too long, the tape is running out, and we haven’t covered enough. All right. I’ll quickly tell it. Martha Glaser asked Al to go over with Erroll when Erroll made his first trip to Europe. It was basically to play at the Olympia Theater in Paris, which was the place, like the Palace Theater in vaudeville in America. The man who ran the Olympia was a notoriously tough gangster type named – oh gosh. Bruno Coquatrix. Al had learned French perfectly when he was studying at the Sorbonne and hanging…

Coquatrix explained this through the interpreter. Al said, “I’d like to see the contract.” Coquatrix said sure, handing it to him, because he knows this guy doesn’t speak French. Al glances quickly through it, takes a deep breath, and, as Erroll loves to tell the story, he let loose a blast, an absolute blast, of gutter French gangster slang such as Coquatrix couldn’t imagine any American would know, but which Al knew. He laid Coquatrix out, called him everything in the book, including a cicatrix, which means a…
